abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Lung cancer predominantly affects older adults who already experience comorbidities and are at increased risk of drug–drug interactions (DDIs) due to polypharmacy. Traditional DDI assessments often do not fully capture complex co‐medication patterns observed in real‐world practice due to the risk of introducing confounding factors. This study used U.S. Optum claims data from 2019 to 2024 to characterize co‐medication patterns in predominately non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients and map enzyme‐ and transporter‐mediated liabilities across commonly used medications, chemotherapy agents, and biomarker‐driven therapies. Potential DDI liabilities were further prioritized using a semi‐quantitative clinical framework based on perpetrator strength, substrate sensitivity, narrow therapeutic index status, and available evidence. Frequently used medications included disease‐specific supportive therapies such as ondansetron and dexamethasone, as well as treatments for common U.S. comorbidities such as cardiovascular and endocrine disorders. Many of the co‐medications were substrates, inhibitors, and inducers of pathways critical for NSCLC treatments such as CYP3A, CYP2D6, P‐gp, and OATP1B and additional risks were identified when giving treatments with acid‐reducing agents or QT‐prolonging drugs. These findings demonstrate how integrating real‐world data (RWD) can strengthen DDI assessment by improving clinical trial design, informing risk‐mitigation strategies, and supporting more patient‐centric drug development.

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Drug–drug interaction (DDI) assessments during drug development primarily rely on in vitro studies, dedicated clinical DDI studies, as well as static and dynamic modeling. However, these approaches do not fully capture the complex co‐medication patterns encountered by patients with lung cancer in routine clinical practice.

What question did this study address? ○
This study investigated real‐world co‐medication patterns among patients with lung cancer and evaluated potential enzyme‐ and transporter‐mediated DDIs. It also examined whether integrating real‐world medication utilization with mechanistic DDI knowledge could provide a practical framework for prioritizing clinically relevant DDI risks during drug development.

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
This study demonstrates that integrating real‐world claims data with established DDI knowledge enables systematic identification and prioritization of clinically relevant DDIs in lung cancer. The proposed semi‐quantitative framework combines medication prevalence with perpetrator strength, substrate sensitivity, narrow therapeutic index status, and available clinical evidence to support more clinically meaningful DDI risk assessment.

How might this change clinical pharmacology or translational science? ○
This real‐world data‐driven framework complements traditional DDI assessment by helping prioritize mechanistic and clinical DDI studies, optimize clinical trial design, and support patient‐centric risk management. The framework is readily adaptable to other therapeutic areas, providing a scalable strategy for integrating real‐world evidence into clinical pharmacology, regulatory decision‐making, and patient‐centric drug development.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer‐related mortality in the United States, with estimates that in 2025 there will be approximately 226,650 new lung and bronchus cancer cases and 124,730 related deaths [1]. Lung cancer predominately affects older adults, with most patients at diagnosis being 65 years or older [1]. While lung cancer is classified as either non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) or small cell lung cancer (SCLC), a majority of patients (about 87%) tend to be diagnosed with NSCLC.

Patients with lung cancer often have at least one or more comorbid conditions, which can impact medication utilization [2]. Polypharmacy is exceedingly common in conditions such as cancer, placing patients at elevated risk for drug–drug interactions (DDIs) that can alter exposure, efficacy, or safety [3, 4]. In fact, one outpatient study found that in the 267 patients they evaluated, about 90% had at least one DDI [5]. These DDIs can lead to serious adverse effects or even reduce treatment benefits, which can be detrimental in patients already inflicted by such a serious condition.

In drug development, DDI implications are dependent on the investigational drug being a victim or perpetrator of the interaction. Investigational drugs that are victims of a DDI may have altered exposure resulting in toxicity or reduced efficacy and necessitating dose adjustments. Conversely, perpetrators of a DDI can modify the exposure of co‐medications, creating safety challenges for those with comorbidities that require such therapies. Thus, understanding the type of DDI risk that the investigational drug may have or is responsible for is essential in planning further evaluations during development and allowing safe clinical use.

Despite these consequences, traditional DDI assessment within drug development has limitations in capturing this risk. Regulatory guidance (ICH M12) emphasizes evaluation of enzyme‐ and transporter‐mediated interactions through in vitro assays, modeling, and dedicated clinical studies [6]. However, in vitro and modeling approaches do not account for complex medication patterns, and clinical trials often exclude patients on multiple concomitant drugs to minimize confounding effects. As a result, real‐world DDI risks in target patient populations are not well characterized.

Real‐world data (RWD), including electronic health records (EHRs), insurance claims, and patient registries, offers an innovative opportunity to bridge this gap. Claims and EHR databases can capture prescribing patterns, patient demographics, and comorbidities in specific populations [7]. By analyzing RWD for co‐medication use and identifying medications that are CYP or transporter substrates/inhibitors/inducers, we can gain better insights into DDI risk in specific disease cohorts [7]. RWD also provides information on the prevalence of specific medication utilization in real‐world practice. This information allows those involved in drug development and regulatory agencies to determine how clinically meaningful a potential DDI can be, allowing for further evaluation. Recent studies have applied this approach in other diseases (e.g., multiple sclerosis and breast cancer) to inform DDI assessment during drug development [7]. Integrating RWD allows for enhanced trial design, improved patient safety, and supports regulatory decision‐making.

This research utilizes U.S. claims data and known DDI liabilities and applies a RWD‐based framework to NSCLC. Identifying commonly utilized concomitant medications in this population and determining their enzyme‐ and transporter‐mediated liabilities helps to inform clinical trial design and DDI risk management strategies. This approach aims to complement traditional DDI evaluation, inform clinical trial design, and support patient‐centric drug development in lung cancer.

sec.title: Cohort Selection and Data Source
sec.p: A retrospective cohort study using a large de‐identified U.S. health insurance claims database (Optum) was evaluated from 2019 to 2024. The database contains fully adjudicated medication claims from patients across all 50 states, including both commercial insurance and Medicare Advantage enrollees. For data completeness, only patients with continuous enrollment in a health plan during the study period were included.

Eligible patients consisted of adult patients (age 18 or older) with at least one diagnosis of lung cancer identified by ICD‐10 codes under malignant neoplasm of the bronchus and lung C34.X (Table S1) during the study period of 2019 to 2024. Lung cancer subtype was not available in the data provided; thus, to reduce potential inclusion of patients with SCLC, treatment‐based proxies were used as an exclusion criterion. Therefore, patients with claims for etoposide, lurbinectedin, topotecan, or tarlatamab (Hallmark treatment for SCLC) [8] were excluded. Additionally, patients were required to have continuous enrollment for at least 6 months prior to and 6 months following their lung cancer diagnosis claim to capture baseline and follow‐up medication use.

To evaluate the robustness of this cohort definition, a sensitivity analysis was conducted comparing medication prevalence and rankings in the primary analysis cohort with those in a more restrictive cohort identified using an NSCLC treatment‐based proxy approach. Specifically, we used lung cancer patients with a 60 day post‐diagnosis cutoff and then applied the Patel et al. algorithm [9] to identify patients with NSCLC from our original lung cancer cohort.

Medications with a prevalence greater than or equal to 0.2% (N ≥ 12) in the Optum cohort during the observation period of 3 months post‐diagnosis were included in this analysis. Selection of this observation window was informed by comparisons of the most frequently prescribed medications during the 6 months before diagnosis, the first 3 months after diagnosis, and the subsequent 3–6 months after diagnosis (Tables S8 and S9). Evaluation at 3 months provided for better assessment of changes in prescription patterns post‐diagnosis, allowing for appropriate time in which patients start receiving treatments and supportive therapies. Changes in prescribing patterns across the observation periods were particularly evident for supportive‐care medications, including ondansetron, dexamethasone, prochlorperazine, and oxycodone (Table S9). Nevertheless, 21 of the 25 most frequently prescribed medications remained among the top 25 during both post‐diagnosis periods, indicating substantial overall stability in the most commonly used medications. Those with a prevalence less than this threshold were excluded from this assessment due to prevalence being so low (N < 13) and to reduce noise from infrequently utilized medications. These medications, as they are typically used for supportive care or comorbid conditions, were defined as concomitant medications in this analysis and evaluated for their potential to have DDIs with lung cancer therapies.

sec.title: Selection of Chemotherapeutic Agents and Biomarker‐Driven Therapies
sec.p: Current clinical practice recommendations for lung cancer were identified using the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology for NSCLC (Version 3.2025). From these guidelines, all small molecule drugs classified as systemic therapies and molecular or biomarker‐directed therapies were extracted for inclusion in this analysis. Protein‐based therapeutics, including monoclonal antibodies and antibody‐drug conjugates, were excluded due to their minimal involvement as perpetrators in enzyme‐ or transporter‐mediated drug interactions [6].

sec.title: Mapping of Drug–Drug Interaction Liabilities
sec.p: Enzyme‐ and transporter‐mediated drug interaction liabilities for each lung cancer therapy and concomitant medication were characterized using a database created by mapping DDI data from multiple sources to identify potential risks. The sources used include individual U.S. Prescribing Information (USPI), FDA drug interaction resources, the Certara Drug Interaction Database (DIDB), the Indiana University Drug Interaction Flockhart Table, and relevant literature identified through PubMed searches. FDA resources were considered the most relevant along with individual USPIs. Other data taken from Certara DIDB, Flockhart Table, and PubMed search results were included for confirmation of substrate/perpetrator classifications with new data being incorporated based on further evaluation and quality control. The evaluation encompassed key metabolizing enzymes, including cytochrome P450 (CYP) and uridine 5′‐diphospho‐glucuronosyltransferases (UGT). Efflux transporters such as P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp), breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), multidrug and toxin extrusion (MATE) and uptake transporters such as organic anion transporting polypeptides (OATP), organic cation transporters (OCT), and organic anion transporters (OAT) were also evaluated for their DDI potential. Each drug was cataloged based on identification as a substrate, inhibitor or inducer for these enzymes and transporters.

sec.title: Prioritization of Drug–Drug Interaction Potential
sec.p: FDA definitions for inhibition and induction strength, as well as substrate sensitivity classifications were used [6]. An inhibitor increases the AUC of a sensitive index substrate via that specific CYP enzyme by ≥ 5‐fold for strong inhibition, between 2 and 5‐fold for moderate inhibition, and 1.25 to 2‐fold for weak inhibition. An inducer decreases the AUC of a sensitive index substrate by ≥ 80% for strong induction, between 50% and 80% for moderate induction, and between 20% and 50% for weak induction. A sensitive substrate is defined as one that has a ≥ 5‐fold increase in AUC when administered with a strong inhibitor due to its metabolism primarily being through that CYP enzyme. A moderately sensitive substrate demonstrates a 2 to 5‐fold increase in AUC when administered with a strong inhibitor. A narrow therapeutic index (NTI) drug is defined as a drug for which small differences in dose or systemic exposure, including blood concentration, may lead to serious therapeutic failure and/or adverse drug reactions [10, 11, 12].

To provide clinical prioritization beyond identification of shared metabolic pathways, Tables 4 and 6 include potential tiers of DDI potential based on perpetrator strength and substrate sensitivity or NTI status. For CYP‐mediated interactions, Tier 1 included a strong inhibitor or inducer with a sensitive or NTI substrate. Tier 2 included a strong perpetrator with a moderately sensitive substrate or a moderate perpetrator with a sensitive or NTI substrate. Tier 3 included a moderate perpetrator with a moderately sensitive substrate.

Transporter inhibitors and substrates in Tier 1 were classified using FDA criteria that incorporate both in vitro evidence and specified clinical pharmacokinetic evidence. For transporter inhibitors, the FDA criteria were as follows: P‐gp inhibition required evidence of in vitro inhibition and a ≥ 1.5‐fold increase in the AUC of sensitive substrates; BCRP inhibition required in vitro inhibition and a ≥ 1.5‐fold increase in sensitive substrate AUC; OATP1B inhibition required in vitro inhibition and a ≥ 2‐fold increase in the AUC of at least one recognized clinical substrate; OAT1/3 inhibition required in vitro inhibition and a ≥ 1.5‐fold increase in the AUC of at least one recognized clinical substrate; and OCT2/MATE inhibition required in vitro inhibition and a ≥ 1.5‐fold increase in metformin AUC [13].

For transporter substrates in Tier 1, P‐gp substrate classification required evidence of in vitro transport, absence of extensive in vivo metabolism, and a ≥ 1.5‐fold increase in AUC with known P‐gp inhibitors. BCRP substrate classification required evidence of in vitro transport and a ≥ 2‐fold increase in AUC with pharmacogenetic alteration. OATP1B substrate classification required evidence of in vitro transport and a ≥ 2‐fold increase in AUC with known OATP1B inhibitor or pharmacogenetic alteration. OAT1/OAT3 substrate classification required evidence of in vitro transport, a ≥ 1.5‐fold increase in AUC with probenecid, and an unchanged renal excretion fraction of ≥ 0.5. OCT2/MATE substrate classification required evidence of in vitro transport, a ≥ 1.5‐fold increase in AUC with dolutegravir or pyrimethamine, and an unchanged renal excretion fraction of ≥ 0.5 [13].

Other CYP and transporter perpetrators and substrates not prioritized in Tables 4 and 6 are presented in the Supporting text. These include weak or unclassified CYP perpetrators identified by the FDA, as well as additional enzyme‐ and transporter‐mediated perpetrators and substrates identified from other prespecified sources.

Gastric pH‐dependent interactions involving acid‐reducing agents and additive QT‐prolongation concerns were not evaluated in the clinical prioritization and solely listed based on identified information.

sec.title: Management of DDIs
sec.p: Information on the management of drug interactions based on need for dose adjustment, therapy substitution, and monitoring recommendations presented in this research was summarized from individual product USPI and supplemented with typical patterns from clinical practice such as avoiding concomitant use or dose modifications based on observed DDI risk.
